overview: Coles Group is one of Australia's two dominant grocery retailers, operating a national network of 870 supermarkets and 988 liquor stores (Liquorland, Liquorland Cellars) alongside omnichannel digital platforms. Demerged from Wesfarmers in November 2018, Coles generates the large majority of earnings from its Supermarkets segment (fresh food, groceries, general merchandise, Coles Online, Coles 360 retail media and Coles Financial Services), with a smaller and currently underperforming Liquor segment. The former Coles Express fuel/convenience business was sold to Viva Energy in 2019 (transaction completed 2023), and the residual fuel supply agreement with Viva Energy expires in November 2026.

business_model.summary: Coles earns the vast majority of revenue and profit from everyday grocery retailing through a defensive, high-volume, low-margin Supermarkets segment (EBIT margin ~5.7% in FY26), supplemented by a smaller, currently struggling Liquor retail segment. Growth increasingly comes from eCommerce/omnichannel fulfilment, Coles Own Brand/Exclusive to Coles products, and a growing retail media and data business (Coles 360) built on Flybuys loyalty data (50% owned, 10.3m active members).

revenue_streams.name: Other (PSA with Viva Energy, Property, Flybuys share)

business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market grocery and liquor retail; B2B revenue from Coles 360 retail media sold to consumer goods suppliers
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Australia (domestic-only operations; no meaningful international exposure)

competitive_position.market_position: Coles holds roughly #2 position in Australian grocery with an estimated ~28-29% national grocery market share, behind Woolworths (~38-40%); together Coles and Woolworths control an estimated 65-67% of Australian grocery sales, a structure the ACCC's 2024-25 supermarket inquiry characterised as an oligopoly with limited incentive to compete aggressively on price. Aldi holds roughly 9-11% and is the largest discount threat; Costco remains small (~1-2%) but growing. In Liquor, Coles (via Liquorland) competes against market leader Endeavour Group (Dan Murphy's, BWS) and independents.

moat_factors.description: Entrenched two-player market structure with Woolworths gives both incumbents purchasing power, shelf-space control and pricing discipline that is difficult for new entrants to replicate at scale
870 supermarkets and extensive distribution network built over decades; high cost and long lead time for a new entrant to replicate convenient store locations
50%-owned Flybuys program (10.3m active members, +3.5% YoY) drives personalisation, switching costs and underpins the growing Coles 360 retail media business

Two Automated Distribution Centres (Sydney, Brisbane) and two Customer Fulfilment Centres now fully operational and delivering positive EBITDA; a third ADC under construction in Truganina, Victoria (~A$880m), creating a cost and service advantage versus smaller players over time
Exclusive to Coles range (~5,600 products) grew sales 6.1% in FY26, outpacing the broader portfolio and providing margin and differentiation benefits versus private label-driven discounters like Aldi
National buying scale and supplier relationships (8,000+ suppliers) support cost of goods and promotional funding that smaller independents cannot match

weaknesses: Thin EBIT margins (~5.7% Supermarkets) leave limited room for absorbing cost shocks or price wars
Liquor segment is structurally challenged: sales down 3.3% and EBIT down 47.8% in FY26, prompting store closures, job cuts and a strategic overhaul
100% domestic concentration in Australia removes geographic diversification and ties the business entirely to Australian consumer/regulatory conditions

Heightened political, regulatory and reputational scrutiny (ACCC litigation, Senate/parliamentary inquiries, media narrative of 'price gouging') constrains pricing flexibility and increases compliance costs

Reliance on enterprise bargaining agreements and large hourly workforce (115,000+ team members) creates industrial relations and wage-inflation risk, illustrated by the FY26 $235m Fair Work Ombudsman provision

growth_drivers: Supermarkets eCommerce growth (+26.4% in FY26, penetration now 13.6%) via Customer Fulfilment Centres, rapid delivery partnership with Uber Eats, and Click & Collect

Automated Distribution Centre rollout (Sydney and Brisbane operational; third ADC under construction in Truganina, Victoria, ~A$880m, commissioning expected by FY30) driving structural cost-out and availability improvements
Simplify and Save to Invest cost program - delivered $311m of benefits in FY26, tracking toward a $1bn four-year target, funding reinvestment in price/value
Coles 360 retail media and data monetisation - income grew 10% in FY26, a high-margin, capital-light growth avenue built on Flybuys data
Exclusive to Coles/Coles Own Brand expansion (new partnerships with M&S, Grill'd, Gami) and Coles Finest premiumisation (+9.2%) supporting mix and margin
Liquor turnaround plan - integrated food-and-drink store formats, network rationalisation (co-location with supermarkets) and operating model simplification aimed at restoring Liquor profitability
AI/agentic commerce and ChatGPT Enterprise rollout to improve forecasting, rostering, personalisation and team member productivity
Continued store network growth/renewals (13 new supermarkets, 71 renewals in FY26) and store format innovation (Coles Local)

business.risk: Intense duopoly competition and changing consumer behaviour
business.description: Need to continuously match Woolworths/Aldi/Costco on price and value amid cost-of-living pressure, value-seeking behaviour and growth of discounters/online entrants
FY26 Liquor EBIT fell 47.8%; restructuring (store closures, 'hundreds' of corporate job cuts planned for FY27) carries execution risk and near-term cost

business.risk: Execution risk on major capital programs
business.description: ADC/CFC construction and Simplify and Save to Invest program delivery risk - cost overrun, delay or failure to realise projected benefits
Exposure to severe weather events (e.g., Cyclone Narelle), supplier cyber incidents, and biosecurity threats (e.g., Tomato Potato Psyllid) affecting fresh produce availability
Growing digital footprint, AI adoption and third-party dependencies increase exposure to data breaches, ransomware and system outages

financial.description: Low single-digit EBIT margins mean earnings are highly sensitive to small changes in sales growth, cost inflation or promotional intensity

financial.risk: Interest rate and lease liability exposure
financial.description: Large lease liabilities (~$8.1bn) under AASB 16 and interest-bearing debt (~$1.8bn) create exposure to funding cost changes, partly mitigated by BBB+/Baa1 credit ratings and 4.4-year average debt maturity
FY26 dividend payout ratio of 83.2% (ex significant items) limits reinvestment flexibility if earnings growth slows

regulatory.description: Federal Court found in May 2026 that certain Down Down ticketing representations were misleading (though underlying price increases were commercially justified); penalties/compensation remain undetermined and a related class action is ongoing, with further ACCC hearings scheduled for December 2026

$235m additional provision recognised in FY26 (total provision $254m) after the Federal Court upheld the FWO's interpretation of Award provisions for salaried team members; final orders, potential appeals and further remediation payments remain outstanding and uncertain

regulatory.risk: New excessive pricing law and mandatory merger regime
regulatory.description: Australia's grocery excessive-pricing prohibition (effective 1 July 2026) and new mandatory ACCC merger notification regime (effective 1 January 2026) add compliance cost and constrain M&A/pricing flexibility for 'very large retailers' like Coles

regulatory.risk: Ongoing political/parliamentary scrutiny of supermarket pricing
regulatory.description: Heightened regulator, government and public scrutiny of supermarket pricing practices (Senate/ACCC inquiries into cost-of-living and supplier relationships) creates reputational risk and risk of further legislative intervention (e.g., divestiture powers debate, Food and Grocery Code changes)

macro.description: Subdued consumer sentiment, particularly weighing on discretionary categories like Liquor, with promotional intensity elevated across the sector
Middle East conflict and global trade disruption affected fuel, raw material and commodity costs in FY26 and continue to be monitored

macro.risk: Input cost inflation and wage inflation
macro.description: Enterprise agreement renegotiations, award-covered remuneration risk and broader wage inflation pressure cost of doing business
Increasing frequency of floods, cyclones and droughts disrupting supply chain and fresh produce availability/cost

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian grocery retail is a large, mature, low-growth-but-defensive industry (low-to-mid single digit nominal growth driven mainly by inflation and population growth) with structurally high concentration (Coles + Woolworths ~65-67% share) under increasing regulatory and political scrutiny over pricing practices and competition
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low - grocery is a defensive consumer staple with resilient demand through economic cycles; Liquor and general merchandise categories carry somewhat higher discretionary/cyclical sensitivity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate direct (modest net debt, long average maturity, fixed/hedged treasury policy); indirect sensitivity via consumer discretionary spending and cost of capital for ADC/CFC investment programs
key_input_costs: Labour/wages under Enterprise Agreements and Awards

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: Group sales revenue $45,580m (+2.8%), Segment EBIT $2,322m (+9.9% ex significant items), NPAT $1,090m (+1.0%; +13.7% to $1,255m excluding significant items); full-year dividend raised 13% to 78.0 cents fully franked
Recognised an additional $235m provision for the Fair Work Ombudsman salaried team member underpayment matter (total provision $254m) following a September 2025 Federal Court judgment

Federal Court found Coles' 2022-23 Down Down price increases were commercially justified, but certain ticketing representations were misleading; penalties/compensation and a related class action remain unresolved, with further proceedings scheduled for December 2026

Announced completion of a strategic review of the Liquor business; plans to close ~30 stores (including Vintage Cellars/First Choice) while opening ~20 in FY27, cut 'hundreds' of corporate roles, and pursue a more integrated food-and-drink/co-located store strategy
Guided to ~A$1.55bn FY27 capex (ex Coles Capability Centre one-offs) and ~$190m of FY27 one-off program costs (including redundancies), above prior broker expectations
JPMorgan downgraded Coles to Hold/Neutral with an A$23.50 price target
Q1 FY27 trading update showed group sales revenue of ~A$11.20bn (+2.2% YoY), with Supermarkets sales growth moderating from prior-quarter levels
Continued construction of the third Automated Distribution Centre in Truganina, Victoria (~A$880m), on budget and schedule, with automation fit-out underway
Australia's new excessive pricing prohibition for very large grocery retailers under the Food and Grocery Code took effect; ACCC's new mandatory merger notification regime took effect 1 January 2026

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Full Year Results (25 August 2026) and Q1 FY2027 trading update (November 2026)

items.notes: Excludes one-off Coles Capability Centre transition costs; above prior broker/market consensus of ~A$1.30-1.35bn, reflecting continued investment in the Victorian ADC, new stores/renewals and technology

items.metric: Simplify and Save to Invest program benefits
items.target: Cumulative ~$1 billion over four years (FY26 delivered $311m)
items.notes: On track per management; funds reinvestment in customer value and offsets cost inflation
Includes Capability Centre dual-running costs and corporate redundancy costs associated with the Liquor strategic review and above-store function consolidation
Funded in part by a further ~$300 million of investment through end-FY28, alongside technology simplification
Part of the Liquor strategic review; exits non-strategic sites (including Vintage Cellars/First Choice) in favour of co-located Liquorland formats

items.target: On budget, commissioning expected by FY2030
items.notes: External construction complete; automation fit-out with Witron underway; ~15% larger than the existing Sydney/Brisbane ADCs

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Leah Weckert said FY26 demonstrated the value of Coles' long-term strategy, with strong Supermarkets momentum offsetting a Liquor segment that performed below expectations and is now undergoing a structural overhaul (store network optimisation, integrated food-and-drink proposition, simplified operating model). Management expects the external operating environment to remain dynamic in FY27 but expressed confidence in Coles' foundations, continued investment in value, digital/AI and operational efficiency. Early FY27 trading (Q1 sales +2.2%) showed some moderation in Supermarkets growth against a tougher prior-year comparison and heightened FY27 investment/cost targets.

bull_case: Defensive, duopoly-protected earnings base with resilient grocery demand largely insulated from broader macro cycles
Multi-year automation investment (ADCs/CFCs) now largely complete and delivering margin expansion (Supermarkets EBIT margin +43bps to 5.7% in FY26), with a clear further leg via the Truganina ADC
High-margin, capital-light growth optionality from Coles 360 retail media (+10%) and Flybuys data monetisation
eCommerce penetration still has substantial runway (13.6% vs. more digitally-mature global peers), supporting continued revenue growth and operating leverage

Liquor turnaround plan, cost discipline (Simplify and Save to Invest) and rising dividend (78.0cps, +13%) with a high, growing payout support total shareholder return even if earnings growth is moderate
bear_case: Intensifying regulatory and political scrutiny (ACCC litigation, excessive pricing law, parliamentary inquiries) structurally constrains pricing power and raises compliance costs, with real financial exposure still unresolved (FWO remediation, Down Down penalties/class action)
Liquor segment remains a drag with uncertain turnaround timing; restructuring costs (~$190m in FY27) and store closures create near-term earnings volatility
Thin, low-single-digit EBIT margins leave limited buffer against cost inflation, wage pressure or renewed price competition from Aldi/Costco/Woolworths
100% Australia-concentrated, ex-growth mature market limits structural top-line growth to population growth plus modest inflation/share gains

Rich capex program (~A$1.55bn FY27 guidance, plus additional store/technology investment) weighs on free cash flow and could pressure the already-high (~83%) dividend payout ratio if earnings growth disappoints
